proposals.title: Encouragement
proposals.content: He leapt out in front of me. I lifted my head. He did it again, closer. I ducked before he landed, which apparently counts as encouragement.
proposals.review: Conditional proposal. Selma is the foreground spectator, not the airborne animal. This changes the central relationship from her own Ocean21 surfing mishap to an escalating display directed at her. Repeated jumps and intention are fictional. Hold if it still feels too close to the spent aerial-play event.

media.context: California sea lion frolicking near the rookery at San Miguel Island, California. Scientists combined the results of sea lion pup counts in the Channel Islands, aerial surveys of sea lion rookeries, survival rates and other information to reconstruct the growth of the sea lion population from 1975 to 2014. They gained enough insight into the dynamics of the population to fill in gaps from a few years with little data. California sea lion breeding group at San Miguel Island, California. Adult males are defending territory, females are tending to their pups, and pups are playing amongst themselves. proposals.title: The voice I turned for
proposals.content: He roared behind me. I waited with my nose toward the water. When he stopped, I heard my pup. That was the voice I turned for.
proposals.review: Propose. The large open-mouthed male, female facing another direction and nearby pups supply the conflicting voices. The actual call, pause and recognition are imagined. This develops Selma's established maternal recognition rather than making a breeding male an assumed babysitter.

media.alt: California Sea Lion Rookery, Photo credit: Sharon Melin
media.context: Adult male California sea lions are identified by their large size, dark brown fur and conspicuous crest on their forehead. Adult females are blonde to light brown and are smaller than the adult males. Pups are dark brown to black. California sea lions have now reached those levels, according to the new assessment by scientists from NOAA Fisheries’ Alaska Fisheries Science Center and Southwest Fisheries Science Center. proposals.title: In the middle
proposals.content: I went under them to get ahead. Came up with my chin nearly on somebody's back. They kept swimming, and for a few breaths I forgot I was trying to pass.
proposals.review: Propose. Raised head between close companions is the exact visual premise. Diving underneath and easing out of the contest are imagined. The story develops the established racing flaw into temporary attachment; it does not repeat paired breath-matching.

Credit: NOAA Fisheries/Amy Brossard (Permit #14450) Photo-ID research provides us with information about the social structure of marine mammals. Social structures may vary by species, population, and location. For example, some species, like large sei whales are routinely photographed in smaller social groups of one to five animals, but smaller cetaceans, like spinner dolphins , often travel in much larger groups of a few hundred or more. proposals.title: The yellow thing
proposals.content: Caught the yellow thing before it drifted away. It crumpled between my teeth. I came up to spit it out. It came up with me.
proposals.review: Hold image quality pending lead decision. The debris encounter is explicit and distinct, with no suffering punchline or invented rescue. The attempted rejection is fictional. This soft 750-pixel source must not pass because the story is interesting.

media.alt: A dolphin upright in the water with its head above water and an empty yellow and white potato chip bag sticking out the side of its mouth..
media.context: Common bottlenose dolphin in Biscayne Bay, Florida with debris. Credit: NOAA Fisheries/Jesse Wicker (Permit #779-1633) Marine debris is any human-made material that ends up in our waterways like microplastics, soda cans, plastic bags, larger discarded items, and more. Marine mammals can become entangled in some of these items like discarded ropes, fabric, or plastic which can become embedded in the animal’s skin as it grows. In addition, animals often ingest discarded plastic items and bags, which can lead to serious internal injury—like tearing the digestive tract—and causing blockages. media.alt: California Sea Lion Rookery, Photo credit: Sharon Melin
media.context: Adult female California sea lion nursing her newborn pup at San Miguel Island, California. The brand on her left shoulder is a permanent brand that identifies her for survival and reproductive rate studies. Marine conditions since 2012 have illustrated that. An unusual marine heat wave off the West Coast known as “the blob” combined with an El Niño climate pattern reduced pup production and survival , with thousands of malnourished pups stranding on Southern California beaches. NOAA Fisheries declared the elevated number of deaths an Unusual Mortality Event in 2013 . The first sighting in the water is usually of the round head. The fore flippers are small and placed far forward with five long, clawed digits. The longer hind flippers are used for locomotion under water but cannot be turned forward as with sea lions. Harbor seals wriggle and hunch to travel on land.
